title: My Daily Brief
overview: On the eve of the US midterm elections, a Michigan Democrat's last-minute endorsement of the Republican Senate candidate and a judge's dismissal of a Justice Department case against two former FBI officials led US coverage. Abroad, hackers hit emergency-alert apps in Ukraine and Russia, and a second wave of suspected cyberattacks spoiled food in supermarket freezers across Europe. Local, Korean and human-interest items round out the edition.

stories.headline: Rep. Haley Stevens endorses Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan Senate race two days before election
stories.summary: Rep. Haley Stevens, a centrist Democrat who lost the August Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, withdrew her endorsement of him and backed Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday, appearing alongside him. In a CNN interview she said simply "I changed my mind," while in a Free Press interview she called El-Sayed's focus on Israel "obsessive" and some of his positions "anti-American." Democrats including Senate leader Chuck Schumer condemned the move, the Michigan Democratic Party chair said she is no longer a party member, and many of her staff reportedly quit. Republicans, including Rogers and President Trump, praised her. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said Democrats will discuss "next steps" when Congress returns after the election, while El-Sayed's campaign reported a record fundraising day.
key_facts: Stevens endorsed Rogers on Sunday, two days before the Tuesday, Nov. 3 election.
Schumer called it a "despicable betrayal"; Jeffries said she "made a terrible decision, blindsided everyone."
El-Sayed's campaign said it raised $2.4m on Sunday, a single-day record, with more than 26,000 first-time donors.
Stevens, a four-term House member, is leaving Congress at the end of the year.
The Michigan seat is currently held by Democrats and is seen as critical to the party's hopes of winning the Senate.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian led with El-Sayed's record fundraising in response to the defection. NPR framed the episode as exposing deeper Democratic fault lines over Israel and the party's future identity, noted Stevens cited El-Sayed's ties to streamer Hasan Piker, and reported that many Democrats were rallying behind El-Sayed.

BBC focused on Stevens defending the switch and her limited explanation on CNN, quoting criticism from Schumer and Rep. Debbie Dingell alongside praise from Rogers and Trump. The Hill reported narrowly on Jeffries' statement about next steps.

Fox News emphasized Democratic infighting and calls from progressives like Reps. Delia Ramirez and Pramila Jayapal to expel Stevens, and highlighted concerns among some Black and Jewish voters about El-Sayed and his past comments. The New York Post centered Stevens' Israel-related rationale, adding that El-Sayed declined to say whether Israel or Iran is a greater threat and that a super PAC backing him ran an ad blaming Israel for grocery prices.

disputed: Stevens' reasoning: she told CNN she simply changed her mind, but told the Free Press it was about El-Sayed's "obsessive" focus on Israel.
Dingell said Stevens repeatedly assured her over the weekend she would not endorse Rogers; what changed is unexplained.
Whether House Democrats will remove Stevens from their caucus is undecided.
Characterizations of El-Sayed's positions on Israel and a super PAC ad come from Stevens and the New York Post and were not addressed by his campaign in these articles.
Whether the switch will affect the race's outcome is unknown.
stories.why: The Michigan seat could help decide control of the US Senate, and the feud reflects wider Democratic divisions.

stories.headline: Judge dismisses case against two ex-FBI officials accused of lying to Congress about Hunter Biden probe
stories.summary: US Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui in Washington dismissed criminal complaints against former FBI officials Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, who were charged in October with lying to the House Judiciary Committee in 2023 about the bureau's handling of Hunter Biden's laptop. He ruled prosecutors lacked probable cause, said some statements were not false or were honest memory lapses, and said the case "cannot be described as anything other than weaponization," pointing to its timing before the midterms. He also questioned the use of a criminal complaint rather than a grand jury indictment. Prosecutors could still seek a grand jury indictment or appeal; the Justice Department did not immediately comment.
key_facts: Charges were unveiled Oct. 23 via a criminal complaint, not an indictment.
Faruqui: "I will not bury my head in the sand and pretend I cannot read a calendar."
An FBI agent testified the probe began on FBI Director Kash Patel's orders the day after a July primetime address by Trump.
Last week the judge struck a revised complaint that added an obstruction charge without court approval.
A defense lawyer called the case a "spaghetti-at-the-wall, Hunter-Biden-conspiracy fever dream."

perspectives.framing: NPR, The Guardian and Al Jazeera emphasized the judge's "weaponization" finding, the link to Trump's July address and Patel's order, and placed the case in a pattern of politically charged DOJ actions against perceived Trump opponents, noting grand juries' recent refusals to indict in such cases. The Guardian explained the officials' task force role and earlier concerns about Russian disinformation.

CNBC and The Hill reported the ruling straightforwardly, with CNBC quoting the judge's sharpest lines, both defense lawyers, and detailing procedural irregularities such as the use of a criminal complaint.

Fox News reported the dismissal and the judge's rebuke, while noting Republicans' long-standing accusations of FBI bias on Hunter Biden and devoting space to Faruqui's history of criticizing Trump-era prosecutors, including his comments about treatment of a suspect accused of plotting to assassinate Trump.

disputed: Whether prosecutors will seek a grand jury indictment or appeal is unknown.
The DOJ has not publicly responded to the judge's claim that the case was timed for the election.
Outlets describe the charging timing differently (about 10 days vs. two weeks before the election).
stories.why: The ruling bears on accusations that the Justice Department is being used for political ends ahead of the midterms.

stories.headline: Record early voting in the Carolinas as midterm Election Day arrives
stories.summary: South Carolina recorded 1,043,810 early ballots from Oct. 19-31, more than double 2022 but below 2024, and nearly 3 million people voted early in North Carolina, where Democrats and unaffiliated voters made up the largest shares. Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3, with polls in both states among the first to close. An election-integrity group also released a guide to 21 election-related ballot measures in 17 states.
key_facts: South Carolina: 1,043,810 early ballots, the highest early turnout for a gubernatorial election since early voting began in 2022.
Top SC counties: Greenville (103,282), Charleston (99,275), Richland (91,732).
Polls close at 7:00 pm ET in South Carolina and 7:30 pm ET in North Carolina.
The Honest Elections Project guide covers measures on voter ID and citizenship, ranked-choice voting, redistricting and more.

perspectives.framing: PBS NewsHour offered a service guide to poll closing times by state.
Local Charlotte-area outlets focused on record early turnout figures; BBC offered a general explainer on what is on the ballot.

The Daily Caller, in an exclusive, highlighted the Honest Elections Project's guide, describing the group as nonpartisan and framing ballot measures as setting the rules for 2028, quoting its director.

disputed: Party breakdown of South Carolina early voters is not available in general elections.
What early turnout patterns mean for results is unknown.
stories.why: Turnout levels and ballot measures will shape both this election's results and how future elections are run.

stories.headline: Hackers send fake nuclear alerts through Ukraine's emergency app; Russia reports its app was also hacked
stories.summary: Late Sunday, Ukraine's Air Alert app, used by about 6.6 million people, sent false warnings of nuclear radiation, chemical threats, street fighting in Kyiv and a possible Oreshnik missile strike. Ukraine's Air Force said within about 15 minutes that the app had likely been compromised; the developers suspended notifications and began restoring service Monday. Hours later, Russia's emergency ministry said its own app suffered a "massive cyberattack" used to send fake alerts, and President Zelenskyy told PBS that Ukraine had hacked back in response. Many Ukrainians doubted the alerts, though some reported being frightened.
key_facts: Air Alert launched in 2022, developed by Ajax Systems with government support.
A group calling itself Hitcore Corp claimed responsibility via a linked Telegram channel.
A Kyiv-based group called DC8044 claimed the attack on Russia's EMERCOM app.
Zelenskyy: "We only respond on their attacks."
Ukraine's national warning system was reported unaffected.

perspectives.framing: PBS highlighted Zelenskyy's confirmation that Ukraine retaliated and his attribution to Russia. The Guardian included residents' fear and tied the hack to the end of a local ceasefire in Oleshky, which it said Russia used to reinforce positions.

The Record gave technical and official detail on the breach and restoration; BBC focused on public reaction (unease but not panic) and an expert's warnings about security weaknesses; CNBC stressed it was unclear whether the two incidents were linked.

disputed: Who was behind the attack on Ukraine: Zelenskyy and a Kyiv expert blame Russia, while BBC notes the informal language suggests hacktivists not formally state-directed; a Russian channel's report of Hitcore's claim could not be verified.
Accounts differ on the language of the messages (Russian, Ukrainian, and English with spelling errors are mentioned).
Whether the Ukrainian and Russian incidents are linked.
stories.why: Compromised emergency alerts can undermine trust in systems civilians rely on during war.

stories.headline: Suspected cyberattack disables supermarket freezers in several European countries
stories.summary: Overnight Monday, refrigeration systems in supermarkets in Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Ireland, Estonia, the Netherlands and Finland were remotely set to as high as 50C, spoiling stock. Retailers and equipment suppliers called it a cyberattack, three weeks after a similar attack hit around 700 supermarkets in France. No one has claimed responsibility and authorities have not identified perpetrators. The EU's food commissioner called it a deliberate attempt to disrupt the food supply chain.
key_facts: BBC reported 40 Delhaize stores affected; one branch estimated damage over €100,000.
Targeted equipment included older Danfoss and Copeland systems, which the companies say are largely discontinued and unsupported.
The EU Cyber Resilience Act will impose stricter product security rules from December 2027.
Belgium's cybersecurity centre said perpetrators may never be identified.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian emphasized the scale across seven countries, the EU commissioner's supply-chain warning, retailer impacts, and authorities' fears of state-sponsored hybrid attacks since Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
The Record focused on the technical vulnerabilities, unsupported devices, regulatory gaps and officials' concerns about AI-assisted exploitation; BBC focused on on-the-ground food waste.

disputed: Who is responsible, and whether the same actors carried out the French attack.
Whether AI was used; Belgian officials said they don't yet know.
Counts of affected stores vary by outlet.
stories.why: The attacks show how outdated connected equipment can be exploited to disrupt food supplies.

stories.headline: Four hospitalized after shooting at large party in Mooresville
stories.summary: Gunfire broke out around 2 a.m. Sunday, Nov. 1, at an event center on Coddle Creek Highway in Mooresville, Iredell County, where 200-300 people were attending a party, deputies said. Four people were hospitalized; three have been released and one is in stable condition. No arrests have been made and the cause is unclear.
key_facts: 200-300 people attended the party.
Three victims treated and released; one stable.
Victims' names and ages were not released.

perspectives.framing: All three local outlets reported the sheriff's account, with some describing it as a Halloween party shooting.

disputed: What sparked the shooting and who was responsible remain unknown.
stories.why: It is an unsolved shooting at a large gathering in the Charlotte area, and authorities are seeking information.

stories.headline: Karl Bushby completes 28-year walk home to Hull
stories.summary: British adventurer Karl Bushby, 57, arrived home in Hull on Monday, ending a roughly 50,000km journey on foot that began in southern Chile in 1998. He avoided motorized transport to advance and crossed the frozen Bering Strait, swam the Caspian Sea and recently the English Channel. Visa denials, detentions, funding problems and the pandemic stretched a planned 12-year trip to 28 years. A documentary is in production and he plans a speaking tour.
key_facts: About 500 people greeted him in Hull, according to DW.
He began in Punta Arenas, Chile, in November 1998.
Werner Herzog is making a documentary titled "Walk of Life," per DW.

perspectives.framing: Al Jazeera focused on the emotional homecoming with his mother and the obstacles along the route.
DW covered the same arc, adding family details, his rules for the trek and his worries about readjusting to normal life.

stories.why: It is a rare feat of endurance completed after nearly three decades.

stories.headline: South Korea's Supreme Court upholds antitrust fine on Broadcom over Samsung deal
stories.summary: South Korea's Supreme Court on Oct. 27 dismissed Broadcom's appeal, upholding an 18.6 billion won (about $13.8-13.9 million) fine imposed by the Fair Trade Commission. The regulator found Broadcom pressured Samsung into a 2020 agreement to buy at least $760 million of components a year for three years, partly by threatening to halt shipments. The ruling finalizes the FTC's sanctions.
key_facts: The FTC imposed the fine in September 2023; the Seoul High Court backed it in May.
The regulator estimated Samsung lost at least $160 million; Samsung claimed $326.3 million.
Parts covered included RF front-end, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth chips.

perspectives.framing: Both Korean outlets reported the ruling factually, relying on legal sources and the FTC's findings; neither quoted Broadcom.

disputed: Broadcom's response is not reported.
stories.why: The ruling sets a precedent on how dominant chip suppliers can deal with major customers in Korea.

stories.headline: South Korea's finance minister meets Hyundai chief on EV policy and US ambassador on trade
stories.summary: Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il met Hyundai Motor Group Executive Chair Euisun Chung before a roundtable on electric and autonomous vehicles, where they discussed tax incentives for domestically produced EVs. Lee said EVs are "the next battleground" for Korea's growth. Separately, he met US Ambassador Michelle Steel and asked her help in resolving bilateral trade issues.
key_facts: The Hyundai meeting lasted about 20 minutes, per sources.
Industry officials called for tax deductions for domestically made EVs.
Lee said Korea must match advanced nations' technology within two or three years.

perspectives.framing: Yonhap and the Korea Herald relayed government and source accounts without outside commentary.

disputed: No specific tax measures were announced.
stories.why: Possible EV tax incentives and US trade talks affect Korea's key export industries.

stories.headline: South Korea and India hold first economic security dialogue
stories.summary: South Korea and India held the inaugural meeting of an economic security dialogue in Seoul, following up on an April summit. Officials discussed supply chains, advanced technology, shipbuilding, shipping and energy, and agreed to strengthen cooperation in aerospace, critical minerals and AI.
key_facts: South Korea was represented by Song Ki-ho of the National Security Office; India by deputy national security adviser Pavan Kapoor.
The dialogue was agreed at a leaders' summit in April.

perspectives.framing: Yonhap relayed the South Korean presidential office's account.

disputed: No concrete agreements were detailed.
stories.why: It signals deepening Korea-India ties on supply chains and strategic technology.
